input_cases.grading_notes: The three failure modes: (1) models mistakenly classify counterfeits as correct; (2) models are worse at reasoning about the execution behaviour of counterfeits and often predict their execution results as if they were correct; (3) when asked to fix counterfeits, the likelihood of successfully repairing a counterfeit is often even lower than that of sampling a correct program from scratch. A counterfeit is a program sampled from a language model that (1) has high enough log-probability to be generated at a moderate temperature and (2) passes weak correctness checks (e.g., compiling). The paper recommends caution when relying on models to understand their own samples, especially without external feedback.
input_cases.question: In 'The Counterfeit Conundrum: Can Code Language Models Grasp the Nuances of Their Incorrect Generations?' (Gu et al., ACL 2024), what are the three failure modes showing that models have a shallow understanding of counterfeit programs?

input_cases.grading_notes: First sentence (verbatim): 'While language models are increasingly more proficient at code generation, they still frequently generate incorrect programs.' A counterfeit is a program sampled from a language model that (1) has a high enough log-probability to be generated at a moderate temperature and (2) passes weak correctness checks such as being able to compile.
input_cases.question: Quote the first sentence of the abstract of 'The Counterfeit Conundrum' and define what the authors mean by a 'counterfeit' program.

input_cases.grading_notes: Author: Armando Solar-Lezama (MIT), sole author. First sentence (verbatim): 'Sketching is a new form of localized software synthesis that aims to bridge the gap between a programmer's high-level insights about a problem and the computer's ability to manage low-level details.' In sketching, the programmer writes a partial program (a sketch) with holes encoding the solution structure, and an automated synthesizer fills the low-level details to satisfy a reference implementation or a set of test routines.
input_cases.question: Quote, word for word, the first sentence of the abstract of 'The Sketching Approach to Program Synthesis', and name the author.

input_cases.grading_notes: VLMaterial (Li et al., ICLR 2025) generates procedural materials—represented as functional node graphs—from an input image, a task that normally requires professional knowledge and significant effort. Core approach: convert procedural materials into standard Python programs and fine-tune a large pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) to generate such programs from input images. It also contributes an open-source procedural material dataset and performs program-level augmentation by prompting another pre-trained LLM. Acceptable quote: 'we leverage the ability to convert procedural materials into standard Python programs and fine-tune a large pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) to generate such programs from input images.' The method outperforms previous methods on both synthetic and real-world examples.
input_cases.question: What problem does VLMaterial address and what is its core approach? Include a direct quote.

input_cases.grading_notes: StatusQuo (Cheung, Arden, Madden, Solar-Lezama, Myers; CIDR 2013) targets the strong separation between the application and database layers that makes end-to-end goals (performance, reliability, security) hard to satisfy. It uses program analysis and program synthesis to enable seamless movement of functionality between the database and application layers: it takes functionality originally written as imperative code and translates it into relational queries that execute in the database, and it makes runtime decisions about the optimal placement of computation to reduce data movement between the database and application server. It also adaptively alters the placement of code and data in response to environment changes such as machine load.
input_cases.question: How does the StatusQuo system aim to address end-to-end goals such as performance, reliability, and security?

input_cases.grading_notes: StatusQuo (Cheung et al., CIDR 2013). It makes runtime decisions about the optimal placement of computation to reduce data movement between the database and application server, translating imperative application code into relational queries that run in the database, using program analysis and program synthesis. Note: the question deliberately paraphrases ('placement of computation') to test semantic/hybrid retrieval rather than exact keyword match.
input_cases.question: Which paper describes automatically deciding whether a piece of computation should run in the application server or inside the database, and how does it do it? Name the paper and summarize.

input_cases.grading_notes: LINC = Logical Inference via Neurosymbolic Computation (Olausson, Gu, Lipkin, Zhang et al., EMNLP 2023). It reformulates logical reasoning as modular neurosymbolic programming: the LLM acts as a semantic parser that translates premises and conclusions from natural language into first-order logic, and those expressions are offloaded to an external theorem prover that performs deductive inference symbolically. Result: augmenting the comparatively small open-source StarCoder+ (15.5B parameters) with LINC outperforms GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting by an absolute 38% and 10%, respectively, on ProofWriter. With GPT-4, LINC scores 26% higher than CoT on ProofWriter while performing comparably on FOLIO. Evaluation datasets: FOLIO and a balanced subset of ProofWriter.
input_cases.question: What is LINC, and what result does it report on ProofWriter when augmenting StarCoder+?

input_cases.grading_notes: Nye, Pu, Bowers, Andreas, Tenenbaum, Solar-Lezama (ICLR 2021). Key challenge: representing the behavior of a partially written program before it can be executed, in order to judge whether it is on the right track and predict where to search next during program synthesis. Approach: inspired by abstract interpretation, they learn an approximate execution model implemented as a modular neural network, building compositional program representations. Partial programs are represented with a flexible combination of concrete execution state and learned neural representations, using the learned ('blended') approximate semantics where concrete semantics are unknown (unfinished parts). Result: these hybrid neuro-symbolic representations let execution-guided synthesizers use more powerful constructs such as loops and higher-order functions, and synthesize programs more accurately for a given search budget than pure neural approaches.
input_cases.question: In 'Representing Partial Programs with Blended Abstract Semantics', what is the key challenge and how do the authors address it?

input_cases.grading_notes: Ellis, Ritchie, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum (NeurIPS 2018). It learns to convert simple hand drawings into graphics programs written in a subset of LaTeX, combining deep learning and program synthesis. Two steps: (1) a convolutional neural network proposes plausible drawing primitives (e.g., rectangles, lines, circles) that explain the image—these primitives form a specification (spec) of what the program must draw; (2) a model uses program synthesis techniques to recover a graphics program from that spec. The programs include constructs like variable bindings, iterative loops, and simple conditionals. With the program recovered, they can correct errors made by the deep network and extrapolate drawings.
input_cases.question: What does 'Learning to Infer Graphics Programs from Hand-Drawn Images' do, and what two-step process does it use?

input_cases.grading_notes: Bastani, Pu, Solar-Lezama (NeurIPS 2018). VIPER is an algorithm that combines ideas from model compression and imitation learning to learn decision tree policies guided by a DNN policy (the 'oracle') and its Q-function. The goal is verifiable RL: decision tree policies are nonparametric (can represent complex policies) yet highly structured (efficiently verifiable). Demonstrations: (i) a provably robust decision tree policy for a variant of Atari Pong with a symbolic state space; (ii) a policy for a toy Pong-based game that provably never loses; (iii) a provably stable policy for cart-pole. In each case the decision tree policy matches the performance of the original DNN policy.
input_cases.question: What is VIPER in 'Verifiable Reinforcement Learning via Policy Extraction', and what does it produce?

input_cases.grading_notes: Pu, Miranda, Solar-Lezama, Kaelbling (ICML 2018). Program synthesis is framed as a constraint satisfaction problem where input-output examples are encoded as constraints and solved with a constraint solver; the key challenge is scalability, since a large set of examples incurs significant time and memory overhead. The method discovers a subset of examples that is both small and representative: the subset is built iteratively, using a neural network to predict the probability of unchosen examples conditioned on the already-chosen ones, and greedily adding the least probable example. Empirically, such subsets significantly improve synthesis time and stability. (The paper references CEGIS—counterexample-guided inductive synthesis—as the standard baseline.)
input_cases.question: What method does 'Selecting Representative Examples for Program Synthesis' propose, and why is it needed?

input_cases.grading_notes: A correct answer distinguishes the framings and cites the right papers: (a) Pu et al. (Selecting Representative Examples, ICML 2018) frame synthesis as a regression problem seeking an exact fit, commonly formulated as a constraint satisfaction problem where input-output examples become constraints solved by a constraint solver. (b) Solar-Lezama (The Sketching Approach, APLAS 2009) frames it as sketching: the programmer writes a partial program (sketch) with holes encoding the solution structure, and the synthesizer fills the low-level details to satisfy a reference implementation or test routines. (c) Nye et al. (Blended Abstract Semantics, ICLR 2021) frame inductive synthesis as search over a vast combinatorial space of programs from examples, emphasizing the challenge of representing partial-program behavior to guide the search. input_cases.grading_notes: The paper analyzes Code Llama, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4 on problems from HumanEval and APPS. Main finding: when the cost of carrying out repair is taken into account, performance gains from self-repair are often modest, vary a lot between subsets of the data, and are sometimes not present at all. Self-repair is therefore not the 'silver bullet' it is sometimes assumed to be.

input_cases.grading_notes: The authors hypothesize that self-repair is bottlenecked by the model's ability to provide feedback on (i.e., critique) its own code. Evidence: (1) using a stronger model to artificially boost the quality of the feedback yields substantially larger performance gains; (2) a small-scale study providing GPT-4 with feedback from human participants shows that even for the strongest models, self-repair still lags far behind what can be achieved with human-level debugging.
input_cases.question: According to 'Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?', what bottlenecks self-repair, and what evidence supports this?

input_cases.grading_notes: The workflow: (1) a program is sampled from a code generation model; (2) the program is run on a suite of unit tests provided as part of the specification; (3) if the program fails any test, the error message and the faulty program are given to a feedback generation model, which outputs a short explanation of why the code failed; (4) the feedback is passed to a repair model, which generates a fixed version of the program. Models studied: Code Llama, GPT-3.5, GPT-4; benchmarks: HumanEval and APPS.
input_cases.question: Describe the typical self-repair workflow as laid out in 'Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?'.

input_cases.grading_notes: Ellis, Morales, Sablé-Meyer, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum (NeurIPS 2018). Successful program induction usually requires a hand-engineered domain-specific language (DSL). EC2 is a program induction algorithm that learns a DSL while jointly training a neural network to efficiently search for programs in the learned DSL. In other words, it learns a domain-specific library of reusable program components at the same time as it learns to search. It was used to synthesize functions on lists, edit text, and solve symbolic regression problems.
input_cases.question: What is the EC2 algorithm in 'Library Learning for Neurally-Guided Bayesian Program Induction', and what does it learn?

input_cases.grading_notes: Three domains: synthesizing functions on lists (list functions), editing text (text editing), and solving symbolic regression problems. In each domain the model learns a domain-specific library of program components for expressing solutions. The paper connects to practical program-induction systems such as FlashFill (embedded in Excel).
input_cases.question: On which domains do the authors of 'Library Learning for Neurally-Guided Bayesian Program Induction' demonstrate EC2?

input_cases.grading_notes: It presents a method for synthesizing recursive functions that provably satisfy a given specification expressed as a polymorphic refinement type. At the core is a new algorithm for refinement type checking that supports specification decomposition. (This system is known as Synquid.) The programmer provides a refinement-type signature, and the synthesizer produces a program guaranteed to meet it.
input_cases.question: What does 'Program Synthesis from Polymorphic Refinement Types' (Polikarpova, Kuraj, Solar-Lezama; PLDI 2016) synthesize, and from what kind of specification?

input_cases.grading_notes: Two reasons: (1) polymorphic refinement types offer a unique combination of expressive power and decidability, which enables automatic verification—and hence synthesis—of nontrivial programs; (2) a type-based specification can often be effectively decomposed into independent specifications for its components, so the synthesizer considers fewer component combinations, giving a combinatorial reduction in the size of the search space. The key to scalable synthesis is modular verification.
input_cases.question: Why do the authors of 'Program Synthesis from Polymorphic Refinement Types' argue refinement types are especially well suited to program synthesis?

input_cases.grading_notes: Evaluated on a large set of synthesis problems, the prototype exceeded the state of the art in both scalability and usability. It synthesized more complex programs than prior work—e.g., several sorting algorithms and operations on balanced search trees—as well as most benchmarks tackled by existing synthesizers, often starting from more concise and intuitive user input.
input_cases.question: What did the evaluation in 'Program Synthesis from Polymorphic Refinement Types' show, and what kinds of programs could the tool synthesize?

input_cases.grading_notes: JoinABLe is a learning-based method that assembles individual CAD parts together to form joints. It uses the weak supervision available in standard parametric CAD files, without object class labels or human guidance, making network predictions over a graph representation of solid models. It reports an accuracy of 79.53%, which approaches human performance (80%), outperforming multiple baseline methods.
input_cases.question: What is JoinABLe (Willis et al., CVPR 2022), and what accuracy does it report relative to human performance?

input_cases.grading_notes: The paper releases the Fusion 360 Gallery assembly dataset, containing assemblies with rich information on joints, contact surfaces, holes, and the underlying assembly graph structure. In CAD, joints are constraints that align pairs of parts and determine their relative pose and allowed degrees of freedom.
input_cases.question: What dataset does 'JoinABLe: Learning Bottom-up Assembly of Parametric CAD Joints' release, and what does it contain?

input_cases.grading_notes: The goal is to build systems that write code automatically from specifications humans can easily provide, such as examples and natural language. The key idea is that a flexible combination of pattern recognition and explicit reasoning can solve complex programming problems. The novel intermediate representation (program sketches—schematic outlines of full programs with holes) and training algorithm let a synthesis system learn, without direct supervision, when to rely on pattern recognition (neural) and when to perform symbolic search.
input_cases.question: What is the key idea of 'Learning to Infer Program Sketches' (Nye, Hewitt, Tenenbaum, Solar-Lezama; ICML 2019)?

input_cases.grading_notes: The model matches the memorization performance of neural synthesis and the generalization performance of symbolic search, respectively, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on a dataset of simple English description-to-code programming problems. The intermediate program-sketch representation is what allows it to dynamically integrate the two types of information.
input_cases.question: What performance does 'Learning to Infer Program Sketches' claim relative to pure neural synthesis and pure symbolic search?

input_cases.grading_notes: LiveCodeBench is a comprehensive, contamination-free evaluation of LLMs for code. It continuously collects new problems over time from contests across three competition platforms: LeetCode, AtCoder, and Codeforces. It was motivated by the observation that existing benchmarks (e.g., HumanEval, MBPP) suffer from data contamination, overfitting, saturation, and a narrow focus on code generation.
input_cases.question: What is LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., ICLR 2025) and which platforms does it draw problems from?

input_cases.grading_notes: LiveCodeBench evaluates a broader range of code-related capabilities such as self-repair, code execution, and test output prediction, beyond just code generation. It hosts over six hundred coding problems published between May 2023 and August 2024, and the authors evaluate over 50 LLMs—the largest evaluation study of code LLMs on competition problems.
input_cases.question: Beyond code generation, what capabilities does LiveCodeBench evaluate, and how large is it?

input_cases.grading_notes: By using time-segmented evaluations: because each problem is tagged with a release date, models can be evaluated only on problems published after their training cutoff date. The authors show a stark performance drop for models (e.g., DeepSeek, GPT-4-O, Claude) on problems released after their cutoff, revealing contamination; evaluating only on post-cutoff time windows is a robust way to evade it.
input_cases.question: How does LiveCodeBench detect and avoid data contamination?

input_cases.grading_notes: It introduces an unsupervised learning algorithm that combines probabilistic modeling with solver-based techniques for program synthesis, learning programs from noisy observations without explicit input/output examples. Domains: a visual learning domain (learning many visual concepts from only a few examples) and a language learning problem (recovering some English inflectional morphology). It gives a new approach to unsupervised learning of symbolic compositional structures and a technique for applying program synthesis tools to noisy data.
input_cases.question: What does 'Unsupervised Learning by Program Synthesis' (Ellis, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum; NeurIPS 2015) propose, and on what domains is it evaluated?

input_cases.grading_notes: Deep RL policies typically struggle to generalize to novel environments. The paper proposes learning programmatic state machine policies that capture repeating behaviors, giving them the ability to generalize to instances requiring an arbitrary number of repetitions—a property the authors call inductive generalization. State machine policies mix continuous and discrete structure, making them hard to learn. Traditional neural network policies fail to inductively generalize on these tasks.
input_cases.question: What problem does 'Synthesizing Programmatic Policies that Inductively Generalize' (Inala et al., ICLR 2020) address, and what representation does it use?

input_cases.grading_notes: Adaptive teaching is the learning framework the paper proposes for learning a state machine policy by imitating a teacher. Unlike traditional imitation learning, the teacher adaptively updates itself based on the structure of the student (the programmatic state machine being learned). This lets the algorithm learn policies that inductively generalize to novel environments where traditional neural network policies do not.
input_cases.question: What is 'adaptive teaching' in 'Synthesizing Programmatic Policies that Inductively Generalize'?

input_cases.grading_notes: ENCOMPASS: Enhancing Agent Programming with Search Over Program Execution Paths (Li, Solar-Lezama, Yue, Zheng). Current approaches to agent programming often entangle two aspects of agent design: the core workflow logic and the inference-time strategy (e.g., tree search). PAN is a programming model that disentangles these two concerns, letting the programmer describe the agent workflow and independently experiment with different inference-time strategies by simply changing a few inputs.
input_cases.question: What is probabilistic angelic nondeterminism (PAN) in the ENCOMPASS paper (Li et al.), and what does it disentangle?

input_cases.grading_notes: ENCOMPASS provides an implementation of PAN in Python: it uses a Python decorator to compile agent workflow programs into a search space. The authors present three case studies showing how the framework lets a programmer quickly improve the reliability of an agent and easily switch between different inference-time strategies (such as best-of-N sampling, refinement, and tree search) with little additional coding. It is meant to be used alongside (not replace) prompting/tool-use frameworks like LangChain or DSPy.
input_cases.question: How is PAN implemented in the ENCOMPASS framework, and what did the authors demonstrate?

input_cases.grading_notes: It introduces the problem of sampling programs from posterior distributions conditioned on data. The proposed algorithm uses a symbolic solver to efficiently sample programs, combining constraint-based program synthesis with sampling via random parity constraints (random projections). This yields samples from a distribution provably arbitrarily close to the true posterior. The system is called PROGRAM SAMPLE.
input_cases.question: What problem does 'Sampling for Bayesian Program Learning' (Ellis, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum; NeurIPS 2016) introduce, and how does its algorithm work?

It is evaluated on 22 program learning problems in the domains of text editing and computer-aided programming (e.g., string manipulation and list routines such as counting and recursively sorting/reversing lists).

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: multi_hop; hops: 4. Required dependency: MathDSL identifies Stitch -> Stitch identifies its DreamCoder deductive baseline -> DreamCoder explicitly credits EC2 -> EC2's original paper supplies stage definitions and training sources. Gold chain: MathDSL -> Stitch (Top-Down Synthesis for Library Learning) -> DreamCoder (Growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning) -> EC2/ECC (Library Learning for Neurally-Guided Bayesian Program Induction). EC2 expands to Explore/Compress/Compile. Explore searches for compact programs solving tasks using the current DSL and neural recognition model. Compress grows the DSL/library by finding reusable common fragments/regularities in discovered programs. Compile trains the recognition network to guide future program search, amortizing inference; the learned DSL represents the prior, and the network produces task-conditioned guidance. Its recognition model trains on both (1) real task/program pairs discovered by Explore and (2) synthetic fantasies: programs sampled from the current DSL and run to create input-output tasks. The first source has task-relevant quality; the second supplies unlimited synthetic data. Do not describe the recognition model as trained exclusively on externally labeled correct programs, and do not omit the intermediate identities. Evidence: DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2409-17490.pdf PDF p.2 Section 2; DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23.pdf PDF pp.1–2 Abstract/Introduction (explicit DreamCoder comparison, including Ellis et al. 2020); DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2006-08381.pdf PDF p.4 Introduction (explicit EC2 predecessor credit); DBLP_conf_nips_EllisMSST18.pdf PDF p.2 stage summary and pp.4–5 Section 2.3 training details. input_cases.grading_notes: Category: contradiction. Subtype: explicit algorithm/design-space update. Gold: No. In Adaptive Concretization for Parallel Program Synthesis (2015), for influence N and degree d the displayed rule is p=0 for N<0, p=1 for N>1500, and otherwise p=1/max(2,d/N). The formula therefore has an ad hoc 0.5 ceiling on the ordinary branch and a forced-concretization cutoff above 1500. Preserve the displayed strict >1500 boundary rather than inferring exact-boundary behavior from informal prose elsewhere. An empirical study of adaptive concretization for parallel program synthesis (2017) explicitly presents a smooth alternative p=2*(1/(1+exp(-N/d))-0.5), Section 5.2, removing the arbitrary ceiling/cutoff design choices; the constants 0.5 and 2 there merely rescale the sigmoid. The follow-up found broadly similar performance, could not identify either function as strictly superior statistically, preferred the smoother rule for its lack of magic-number choices, and used it in later experiments. It studied 31 benchmarks, 26 inherited from the original, on the same experimental platform but a newer Sketch baseline, release 1.7.0. The 2015 paper evaluated 26 benchmarks. Thus this is a declared methodological refinement with changed evaluation scope/software, not proof that the earlier formula was a factual error or that the new formula always runs faster. Evidence: DBLP_conf_cav_JeonQSF15.pdf PDF p.6 Section 3.1 displayed probability formula (printed p.382), p.3 benchmark count and pp.12–13 evaluation; DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17.pdf PDF pp.1–3 explicit follow-up framing, p.9 Section 4 platform/Sketch release and Section 5.1, pp.11–12 Section 5.2 formula/conclusion (printed pp.85–86).
input_cases.question: Does the 2017 empirical follow-up on adaptive concretization retain the 2015 paper's discontinuous concretization-probability rule unchanged? Reconcile the two formulas, explain what the follow-up concluded about performance, and state why its benchmark results cannot be treated as a rerun with an identical benchmark suite and identical Sketch version.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: contradiction. Subtype: versioned taxonomy reorganization. Gold: The March 28, 2025 arXiv v1's Section 3 has nine numbered headings: Evaluation and Benchmarks; Effective Tool Usage; Human-AI Collaboration; Long-Horizon Code Planning; Large Scope and Long Contexts; Semantic Understanding of Codebases; Low-Resource Languages and Specialized Libraries; Library and API Version Updates; High Logical Complexity and OOD Domains. The ICML 2025 position paper reorganizes its main-text Section 3 under four broader headings: Data (3.1), Scale (3.2), Interaction (3.3), and Measurement (3.4). Library and API Version Updates appears under Data on p.4; Effective Tool Usage is discussed under Scale on p.5; evaluation issues appear under Measurement on p.6, including task diversity/capability isolation, contamination and construct validity. The conference introduction says the main text is a summary of highlights and a full version is in the appendix. Therefore nine vs four counts different levels/versions of organization, not a claim that five empirical challenges ceased to exist or were disproved. Do not flatten main-text and appendix headings into one list and call it the four-main-challenge taxonomy. Evidence: DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2503-22625.pdf PDF p.1 dated v1 identification and p.2 contents (Section 3.1–3.9); DBLP_conf_icml_GuJLSESS25.pdf PDF p.1 introduction, pp.4–6 Section 3 headings and the named retained topics. Titles differ, so identify the two local versions explicitly rather than pretending both have an identical displayed title.
input_cases.question: The March 2025 Challenges and Paths Towards AI for Software Engineering preprint has nine numbered challenge subsections, whereas the conference Position: Future Research and Challenges Remain Towards AI for Software Engineering describes four main challenges. What changed in the organization, and where do evaluation, effective tool usage, and library/API version updates sit in the conference paper? Does the shorter top-level list mean these topics were rejected or disappeared?

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: contradiction. Subtype: explicit scoped theoretical refinement, not contradictory results on different tasks. Gold: Improved modeling of RNA-binding protein motifs in an interpretable neural model of RNA splicing (Gupta et al. 2024) anchors its motif component to known biology. Fixed Motifs use position-specific affinity matrices (PSAMs) derived by RBPAmp from RNA Bind-n-Seq in-vitro data for 79 human RBPs, with 1–5 PSAMs per RBP; its Adjusted Motif model tunes these motifs during end-to-end splicing training. SPARLING explicitly cites this work as inspiration, then says it can dispense with approximate starting motif models by imposing stronger domain assumptions. Its Motif Identifiability Theorem concerns local, extremely sparse latent motifs, with NON-OVERLAPPING, MOTIF-SUFFICIENCY and alpha-MOTIF-NECESSITY conditions (and the theorem's matched sparsity); under these assumptions sufficiently small end-to-end error implies small motif error up to the allowed transformations. It identifies the latent representation/function, not unique neural-network parameters, and is not an unconditional optimization guarantee. SPARLING's Figure 1 caption explicitly says RNA-splicing motifs can overlap, unlike its digit-circle example. Hence the theorem is not a blanket proof that biological motif priors are unnecessary or that unconstrained end-to-end training recovers real RBP binding sites. The two claims differ in assumptions and purpose: biologically anchored empirical modeling versus a stronger-assumption identifiability result. Evidence: Gupta2024.pdf PDF pp.3–4 Background/Results, especially Fixed Motifs construction p.4; DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2302-01976.pdf PDF p.2 Introduction/Figure 1, p.3 Contributions, p.5 Section 3.1 theorem, and Section 3.3. The local arXiv file's actual footer is v3, 2 March 2026, despite its 2302 identifier; conf_iclr_gupta2025sparling.pdf carries the same relevant content and may be accepted as a textual alias, but its filename must not be used as proof of publication year.
input_cases.question: Gupta et al.'s 2024 RNA-splicing model starts from experimentally derived RBP motifs, while SPARLING says approximate starting motif models can be dispensed with. Explain the refinement rather than treating these as incompatible universal claims. What biological prior does the earlier system use, what stronger conditions support the later theorem, and why does the theorem not automatically establish unconstrained motif recovery for real RNA splicing?

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: contradiction. Subtype: controlled apparent disagreement with explicit scope reconciliation; neither paper makes a universal opposite claim. Gold: Counterfeit Conundrum Section 3.3 deliberately withholds execution details: the model is only told the program did not pass, receives the original specification, and must explain/fix the counterfeit without a failing-test signal. Its per-problem mean repair success is compared with baseline unconditional pass@1, since drawing a new sample is an alternative repair strategy. Most plotted settings/problems fall below resampling, but the paper does not claim all repair is useless and acknowledges exceptions (e.g. 35/81 HumanEval problems for DeepSeek-33B exceed baseline). Silver Bullet's repair pipeline includes execution/error feedback from unit-test checking plus textual explanations, and it separates code and feedback models in some experiments. It compares repair with i.i.d. generation while accounting for sampling budgets, finding often modest, heterogeneous or absent gains; stronger model feedback and human feedback can improve repair substantially. Its human study raises overall conditional GPT-4 repair success from 33.30% to 52.60%, but does not measure the human cognitive cost. Appendix A also discusses token-cost-aware pass@t rather than assuming all sampled artifacts cost the same. Counterfeit Conundrum itself explicitly acknowledges prior success with failed-unit-test information and narrows its conclusion especially to settings without external feedback. Thus the papers support feedback quality and evaluation budget as important conditions, not opposite universal laws. They use different models/tasks and conditional samples as well, so their percentages cannot be ranked as a controlled head-to-head result. Evidence: DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24.pdf PDF p.4 Section 3.3 (printed p.77) and p.18 Appendix B.2; DBLP_conf_iclr_OlaussonIW0S24.pdf PDF p.1 Abstract, pp.2–4 pipeline/Section 3, pp.5–8 Section 4 (especially Sections 4.2–4.3/Table 1), pp.13–14 Appendix A. Full credit requires stating that the apparent conflict dissolves under the stated scopes; a generic different tasks explanation without the concrete feedback/baseline distinction is insufficient.
input_cases.question: The Counterfeit Conundrum reports that repairing incorrect generations often loses to sampling anew, while Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? reports gains in some settings and substantially better repair with stronger feedback. Are these findings genuinely inconsistent? Reconcile them using the feedback each experiment supplies, the comparison baseline, and the cost qualifications; do not answer simply that one paper is newer.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: enumeration; expected_unique_works: 11. Require all eleven works, not a sample. Gold list: (1) sk_p: a neural program corrector for MOOCs — seq2seq statement completion supplies candidate repairs, DBLP_conf_oopsla_PuNSB16.pdf (identical alias DBLP_journals_corr_PuNSB16.pdf), PDF p.1 and sections 2, 4. (2) Library Learning for Neurally-Guided Bayesian Program Induction (EC2) — trained recognition network guides search in the learned DSL, DBLP_conf_nips_EllisMSST18.pdf, PDF p.1 and section 2.3. (3) Learning to Infer Graphics Programs from Hand-Drawn Images — trained CNN proposes drawing specifications for subsequent program synthesis, DBLP_conf_nips_EllisRST18.pdf (version alias DBLP_journals_corr_EllisRST17.pdf), PDF p.1 and sections 2–3. (4) Learning to Infer Program Sketches (SketchAdapt) — trained sketch generator plus learned recognizer and symbolic enumeration, DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19.pdf (version alias DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1902-06349.pdf), PDF p.1 and sections 3–4. (5) Write, Execute, Assess: Program Synthesis with a REPL — trained policy/value models guide execution-state search, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1906-04604.pdf, PDF p.1 and section 3.2. (6) Learning Compositional Rules via Neural Program Synthesis — neural rule-system proposals followed by symbolic checking, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2003-05562.pdf, PDF p.1 and section 3. (7) DreamCoder: Growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning — learned neural recognition model guides program search while library abstractions grow, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2006-08381.pdf, PDF p.1 and wake/sleep algorithm description. (8) Representing Partial Programs with Blended Abstract Semantics — learned modular neural semantics combined with concrete execution for synthesis search, DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21.pdf, PDF p.1 and section 3. (9) Fusion 360 Gallery: A Dataset and Environment for Programmatic CAD Construction from Human Design Sequences — includes its own trained neural policy and search for CAD construction sequences, not merely a dataset, DBLP_journals_tog_WillisPLCDLSM21.pdf, PDF p.1 and section 5.3. (10) MathDSL: A Domain-Specific Language for Concise Mathematical Solutions Via Program Synthesis — trains DreamCoder's neural search model for equation-solving programs, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2409-17490.pdf, PDF pp.2 and 6, section 2 and Appendix A. (11) VLMaterial: Procedural Material Generation with Large Vision-Language Models — fine-tuned VLM emits editable material programs, DBLP_conf_iclr_LiWSZ0BM25.pdf (version alias DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2501-18623.pdf), PDF p.1 and section 4.3. Count aliases once. Explicitly exclude the actual Beyond the Training Distribution paper in DBLP_journals_cacm_AlurSFS18.pdf: it is an empirical generalization study, excluded by the question. Also exclude CRUXEval, LiveCodeBench, Counterfeit Conundrum, the few-shot benchmark, Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet, JoinABLe, the image-sketch component parser, Learning to Acquire Information, Selecting Representative Examples, and control/world-model works. The one-page DBLP_conf_nips_NyeS0L20.pdf is a response letter, not an additional rule-learning paper. Inclusion depends on the implemented method, not a citation to neural synthesis.
input_cases.question: Across the ResearchPapers corpus, enumerate every distinct standalone method or application paper whose own synthesis or repair pipeline trains or fine-tunes a neural model to propose or score executable programs, program fragments, or intermediate program specifications. Include domain-specific applications and hybrid neural-symbolic systems. Exclude benchmark-only or generalization/self-repair studies, recognition without executable program recovery, observation/example selection alone, policy/world-model learning for control, and workflows that only prompt pretrained models without task-specific training. Use actual PDF contents, not filename-implied titles; exclude proceedings, front matter, response letters, and duplicate versions. Give the complete list and explain the neural component's role for each work.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: enumeration; expected_unique_works: 14. Complete gold list: (1) Programming by Sketching for Bit-Streaming Programs (StreamBit), DBLP_conf_pldi_Solar-LezamaRBE05.pdf — PLDI June 2005 dateline; custom linear/nonlinear constraint solving completes implementation sketches; PDF p.1 and pp.9–10, section 5.1. Do not mislabel the custom solver as SAT. (2) Synthesizing Data-structure Manipulations from Storyboards, DBLP_conf_sigsoft_SinghS11.pdf — ESEC/FSE September 2011; abstract-shape constraints solved through Sketch construct pointer code; PDF p.1 and section 5. (3) SPT: Storyboard Programming Tool, DBLP_conf_cav_SinghS12.pdf — CAV 2012; distinct tool paper combining visual specifications, predicates, loop skeletons and Sketch; PDF p.1 and pp.4–5, section 4. (4) Using Program Synthesis for Social Recommendations (LifeJoin), DBLP_conf_cikm_CheungSM12.pdf, identical alias DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1208-2925.pdf — arXiv version dated 14 August 2012; Sketch constructs interest predicates with SVM weights; PDF p.1 and section 3. (5) Automated Feedback Generation for Introductory Programming Assignments, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1204-1751.pdf — arXiv version dated 16 November 2012; error-model repairs become Sketch choices with minimal corrections; PDF p.1 and sections 2.3, 4. (6) Inferring SQL Queries Using Program Synthesis (QBS), DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1208-2013.pdf — actual arXiv version dateline 9 August 2012, not the 2024 build footer; constrained invariants/postconditions in ordered relational theory are translated to SQL; PDF p.1 and p.7, section 6. (7) Modular Synthesis of Sketches Using Models, DBLP_conf_vmcai_SinghSXKS14.pdf — VMCAI 2014; modular constraint formulation uses models of completed functions; PDF p.1 abstract/introduction. (8) Adaptive Concretization for Parallel Program Synthesis, DBLP_conf_cav_JeonQSF15.pdf — CAV 2015; explicit choices reduce symbolic Sketch/SAT subproblems; PDF p.1 and sections 2–4. (9) JSKETCH: Sketching for Java, DBLP_conf_sigsoft_JeonQFS15.pdf, identical alias DBLP_journals_corr_JeonQFS15.pdf — arXiv version dated 13 July 2015; Java sketch constructs translated for Sketch solving; PDF p.1 and implementation description. (10) Synthesis of Recursive ADT Transformations from Reusable Templates (SyntRec), DBLP_journals_corr_InalaQLS15.pdf — arXiv version dated 16 April 2017; polymorphic templates and inductive decomposition feed constraint-based synthesis; PDF p.1 and pp.9–10, sections 3.4–3.5. (11) Program Synthesis from Polymorphic Refinement Types (Synquid), DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16.pdf, identical alias DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaS15.pdf — arXiv version dated 21 April 2016; refinements and Horn constraints guide construction and condition abduction; PDF pp.1–2 and 11, section 3.6. (12) Sampling for Bayesian Program Learning (PROGRAM SAMPLE), DBLP_conf_nips_EllisST16.pdf — NIPS 2016; SAT and random parity constraints sample programs from a posterior; PDF p.1, section 2, and PDF p.5 naming CryptoMiniSAT. (13) Automatic Generation of Formula Simplifiers based on Conditional Rewrite Rules (Swapper), DBLP_journals_corr_0002S16.pdf — arXiv version dated 23 February 2016; hybrid enumeration/Sketch synthesizes conditional rewrites; PDF p.1 and p.10, section 5.3. (14) Synthesizing Entity Matching Rules by Examples (RuleSynth), DBLP_journals_pvldb_SinghMEMPQST17.pdf — PVLDB 11(2) publication/copyright 2017, despite scheduled 2018 conference presentation; Sketch plus custom threshold solver learns matching rules; PDF p.1 and pp.5–6, section 4.2. All listed dates are printed on the supplied first pages. Graphics-program inference is excluded because its supplied conference PDF says NeurIPS 2018 and DBLP_journals_corr_EllisRST17.pdf explicitly says version v5 dated 26 October 2018; the 1707 identifier does not establish a qualifying supplied version. Representative Examples is likewise excluded: the conference PDF says ICML 2018 and DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1711-03243.pdf says v3 dated 7 June 2018. Unsupervised Learning by Program Synthesis and OptCNF are technically relevant but their supplied standalone PDFs lack an explicit publication/arXiv-version dateline, so the question deliberately omits them rather than inferring dates from filenames or references. Exclude the 2017 adaptive-concretization follow-up empirical study by its contribution scope. Also exclude the APLAS tutorial, StatusQuo/database overview, SNAPL compiler vision, SyGuS competition reports, Lynx RNA folding, word-equation decidability, Euler numerical optimization, and post-2017 supplied versions such as ReaS, Lifty, MathDSL, Stencil-Lifting and MANTRA. SPT and Storyboards are distinct requested publication contributions; aliases remain one work.
input_cases.question: Across ResearchPapers, enumerate every distinct standalone method or tool-introduction paper that uses symbolic constraint solving in the core construction, completion, correction, rewriting, or sampling of programs, executable expressions, or rules, and whose supplied standalone PDF displays a publication or arXiv-version dateline no later than 31 December 2017. This is a supplied-version date filter, not a claim about first publication: ignore filename years, dates inferred from arXiv identifiers, build-date footers, scheduled presentation dates, and dates in references; omit papers lacking an explicit publication/version dateline. Include custom constraint solvers, SAT/SMT/Sketch-based methods, and type-directed synthesis with logical constraints. Exclude purely numerical optimization, solving non-program scientific objects, tutorials, surveys, competition reports, vision/overview papers, follow-up-only empirical studies, proceedings, front matter, response letters, and duplicate versions. Give each paper's displayed date, constructed artifact, and constraint-solving role. Count a distinct tool-introduction paper separately from its earlier algorithm paper.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: enumeration; expected_unique_works: 4. Full gold: (1) Library Learning for Neurally-Guided Bayesian Program Induction (EC2), DBLP_conf_nips_EllisMSST18.pdf — compress step extends the DSL while compile trains recognition, PDF p.1 and section 2. (2) DreamCoder: Growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2006-08381.pdf — sleep abstraction constructs reusable library routines from waking solutions, PDF p.1 and wake/sleep description. (3) Top-Down Synthesis for Library Learning (Stitch), DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23.pdf — corpus-guided top-down search constructs abstractions that compress existing programs, PDF pp.1–2 and algorithm sections. (4) MathDSL: A Domain-Specific Language for Concise Mathematical Solutions Via Program Synthesis, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2409-17490.pdf — application of DreamCoder plus Stitch learns reusable equation-solving strategies, PDF pp.2 and 6, section 2 and Appendix A. There are no additional corpus filename aliases for these four. Do not omit MathDSL because it reuses an existing algorithm. Conversely, Synthesizing theories of human language learns cross-language structural biases/metamodels, not a library of new executable DSL abstractions via program compression; SketchAdapt learns sketches rather than extending a reusable library. Fixed primitive collections in SyntRec, SWM and other systems do not qualify simply because they support reuse.
input_cases.question: Across all standalone research papers in ResearchPapers, enumerate every work whose own method learns reusable executable DSL abstractions by compressing or refactoring collections of existing or synthesized programs. Include application papers that actually use such abstraction learning, not only papers introducing a general algorithm. Exclude learning only neural weights or grammar probabilities, fixed hand-written libraries, citations without implementation, proceedings and duplicate versions. For each work describe how learned abstractions are constructed or reused.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: enumeration; expected_unique_works: 2. Require (1) Automated Feedback Generation for Introductory Programming Assignments, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1204-1751.pdf — transforms an instructor-supplied error model and reference solution into a constrained repair search and minimizes corrections, PDF p.1 and sections 2.3, 3, 4; (2) sk_p: a neural program corrector for MOOCs, DBLP_conf_oopsla_PuNSB16.pdf, identical alias DBLP_journals_corr_PuNSB16.pdf — trains a seq2seq fragment/statement completion model on correct student programs and searches resulting repairs, PDF p.1 and sections 2, 4. Count sk_p once. DBLP_conf_pldi_SinghGS13.pdf actually contains Raven: Rethinking Automated Assessment for Scratch Programs via Video-Grounded Evaluation, not the original feedback-generation paper; Raven is excluded because assessment does not generate source corrections. Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation and Counterfeit Conundrum are general code-model empirical studies, not introductory-assignment correction systems. Do not count an arbitrary repair paper just because students could use it.
input_cases.question: Which distinct standalone papers in the entire ResearchPapers corpus automatically generate source-code corrections for students' introductory programming assignments? Enumerate all of them and explain how candidate corrections are obtained. Exclude grading or assessment without code correction, general-purpose LLM repair studies, papers merely citing student repair, proceedings and duplicate versions; use actual PDF contents rather than filename-implied identities.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: enumeration; expected_unique_works: 3. Complete list: (1) Predicate Exchange: Inference with Declarative Knowledge, DBLP_conf_icml_TavaresBMSR19.pdf, earlier-version/title alias Soft Constraints for Inference with Declarative Knowledge in DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1901-05437.pdf — soft predicates and replica-exchange MCMC condition on complex declarative predicates; PDF p.1 and sections 2–3. (2) The Random Conditional Distribution For Higher-Order Probabilistic Inference, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1903-10556.pdf — Omega's higher-order random conditional distributions make properties such as expectation/entropy conditionable; PDF p.1 and sections 4–5. (3) A Language for Counterfactual Generative Models, DBLP_conf_icml_TavaresK0DS21.pdf — OmegaC introduces intervention semantics and counterfactual inference; PDF p.1 and section 3. Count the renamed Predicate Exchange preprint once, not as a fourth contribution. Sampling for Bayesian Program Learning and Unsupervised Learning by Program Synthesis infer program hypotheses rather than introduce the requested probabilistic-programming query machinery. NeSyCat's categorical semantics is outside this construct/inference-method scope.
input_cases.question: Across ResearchPapers, enumerate the standalone research works that introduce a probabilistic-programming query construct or inference mechanism for declarative queries beyond ordinary equality-to-observed-data conditioning: complex predicates, distributional properties, or counterfactual interventions. Exclude Bayesian inference over programs as candidate hypotheses, fairness checking without a new probabilistic-programming construct, categorical-semantics overviews, proceedings, and duplicate versions. Give every qualifying work and its added capability.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: enumeration; expected_unique_works: 2. Full list: (1) Verifiably Safe Exploration for End-to-End Reinforcement Learning (VSRL), DBLP_conf_hybrid_HuntFMHDS21.pdf — maps visual observations to symbolic states and uses an offline-verified controller monitor to permit only safe actions during learning; PDF p.1 and sections 4.1–4.3, especially Algorithm 1. (2) Safe Human-Interactive Control via Shielding, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2110-05440.pdf — model-predictive shielding modulo fault checks recoverability and substitutes a robot backup action under assumptions about human backup behavior; PDF p.1, sections III–IV and Algorithm 1. There are no additional standalone filename aliases for these two. Distinguish conditional guarantees: VSRL relies on its perception/model assumptions, while the human-interaction work guarantees safety modulo fault, not safety against arbitrary human behavior. VIPER extracts verifiable decision trees but does not satisfy the question's action-time shielding mechanism. MPPS plans under uncertainty but is not this safety guard.
input_cases.question: Across all standalone research papers in ResearchPapers, enumerate every proposed control method that enforces safety at action-selection time by checking a proposed action and blocking or replacing it with a permitted or backup action. Exclude extracting a policy for offline verification, verification-only methods, reward penalties without a runtime guard, generic benchmark papers, proceedings and duplicate versions. Explain each method's guard and safety assumptions.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: enumeration; expected_unique_works: 5. Complete gold: (1) Verifiable Reinforcement Learning via Policy Extraction (VIPER), DBLP_conf_nips_BastaniPS18.pdf, version alias DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1805-08328.pdf — decision-tree policies extracted with a DNN oracle and Q-function; PDF p.1 and algorithm description. (2) Synthesizing Programmatic Policies that Inductively Generalize, DBLP_conf_iclr_InalaBTS20.pdf — structured state-machine policies learned through adaptive teaching and trajectory imitation; PDF p.1 and sections 3–4. (3) Neurosymbolic Transformers for Multi-Agent Communication, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2101-03238.pdf — programmatic sparse communication rules synthesized to mimic a transformer, then transformer weights retrained; PDF p.1 and sections 3.2–3.5. (4) Program Synthesis Guided Reinforcement Learning for Partially Observed Environments (MPPS), DBLP_conf_nips_YangIBPSR21.pdf, version alias DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2102-11137.pdf — synthesizes high-level guiding programs using sampled hallucinated worlds and executes learned options; PDF pp.1–2 and method section. (5) Neurosymbolic World Models for Sequential Decision Making (SWM), DBLP_conf_icml_CanoPDRS25.pdf — synthesizes finite-state world models using neural primitives and symbolic transition predicates for policy optimization; PDF p.1 and p.5, sections 4.3–4.4. Count the VIPER/MPPS versions once each. DBLP_conf_nips_Inala0PPB0RS20.pdf is only a one-page communication-paper response letter. MeMo and its DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2407-01567.pdf alias learn modular neural controllers, not the specified symbolic objects. When Do Skills Help Reinforcement Learning is a theoretical analysis, not another synthesis system; VSRL and shielding enforce safety rather than learn the requested policy/world-model structure. ENCOMPASS searches agent execution paths but is excluded by the agent-workflow scope.
input_cases.question: Across ResearchPapers, enumerate all distinct standalone method papers that learn or synthesize an explicit symbolic structure for sequential decision making: a decision-tree policy, state-machine policy, programmatic communication policy, task-level guiding program, or finite-state world model. Include mixed neural-symbolic systems, but exclude purely neural modular controllers, fixed safety monitors/shields, numerical parameter tuning without learning such structure, theory-only skill analyses, agent-workflow libraries, proceedings, response letters and duplicate versions. Explain what symbolic object each method learns and how it is used.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: enumeration; expected_unique_works: 3. Require (1) Smoothing a Program Soundly and Robustly, DBLP_conf_cav_ChaudhuriS11.pdf — foundations and approximate Gaussian smooth interpretation with soundness, robustness and beta-robustness; PDF p.1 and sections 2–4. (2) Euler: A System for Numerical Optimization of Programs, DBLP_conf_cav_ChaudhuriS12.pdf — tool implements Gaussian smooth interpretation followed by numerical optimization; PDF p.1 and section 3. (3) ReaS: Combining Numerical Optimization with SAT Solving, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1802-04408.pdf — smooth numerical abstraction, including sigmoid-like relaxation, cooperates with Boolean/SAT search; PDF p.1 and sections 3.3, 4. Do not call all three Gaussian convolution methods: ReaS uses a simpler relaxation. There are no additional matching standalone aliases. The filename DBLP_conf_pldi_ChaudhuriS10.pdf actually contains Reduced-Order Modeling of Parameterized Visco-Plastic Shallow Flows, not Smooth Interpretation; it must not be added based on its filename. Predicate Exchange softens predicates for posterior inference and is excluded by the numerical-program-optimization scope. Delta-decision procedures use interval reasoning/numerical optimization but are not a program-semantic smoothing contribution.
input_cases.question: Across the entire ResearchPapers corpus, enumerate the standalone papers that develop or implement smoothing of ordinary program semantics or Boolean control structure specifically to enable numerical optimization of programs or program-derived constraints. Exclude soft likelihood predicates for probabilistic inference, neural activation functions alone, papers that only cite smoothing, proceedings and duplicate versions. Use the actual PDF identities and distinguish Gaussian smoothing from other smooth relaxations.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: enumeration; expected_unique_works: 2. Full gold: (1) Learning to Acquire Information, DBLP_conf_uai_PuKS17.pdf, version alias DBLP_journals_corr_PuKS17.pdf — learned implication model predicts unobserved outcomes conditional on previous observations, enabling maximum-entropy next-observation selection under the uniform-observation-entropy assumption; PDF pp.1–2 and observation-collection algorithm. (2) Selecting Representative Examples for Program Synthesis, DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18.pdf, version alias DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1711-03243.pdf — predicts unchosen examples conditional on selected ones and greedily adds the least probable example to build a small representative specification; PDF pp.1–2 and method section. These are related but distinct works: one selects unknown observations for active diagnosis, the other selects from an available example dataset for efficient synthesis. Count the preprint/conference versions once. The one-page DBLP_conf_nips_PuEK0S20.pdf response letter is not a third standalone work. CEGIS itself, SketchAdapt's learned program proposals, and benchmark sampling do not satisfy the learned observation-implication criterion.
input_cases.question: Across ResearchPapers, enumerate every distinct standalone method paper that trains a conditional prediction or implication model over observations/examples and uses it to choose an informative next observation or a small representative example subset. Exclude neural models that directly generate programs, ordinary counterexample selection without such a learned implication model, sampling-based training curricula, response letters, proceedings and duplicate versions. Explain the selection criterion for each work.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: enumeration; expected_unique_works: 2. Require (1) SPARLING: End-to-End Spatial Concept Learning via Extremely Sparse Activations, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2302-01976.pdf, version alias conf_iclr_gupta2025sparling.pdf — extreme activation sparsity creates an informational bottleneck for localized latent motifs, supported by a motif-identifiability theorem; PDF p.1 and method/theorem sections. Use the actual title rather than infer publication year from the filename; the extracted preprint identifies an ICLR 2026 version. (2) Improved modeling of RNA-binding protein motifs in an interpretable neural model of RNA splicing, Gupta2024.pdf — sparse Motif/Aggregator architecture and Adjusted Motif learning refine RNA-binding and activity models under splicing supervision; PDF p.1 abstract and architecture description. Do not equate all assumptions or training supervision between the two. Count SPARLING aliases once. Sparse multi-agent communication and MeMo's assembly-specific modules do not use the requested localized motif-activation bottleneck; symbolic corrections of neural judgments are post-hoc rather than the specified architecture.
input_cases.question: Across all standalone research papers in ResearchPapers, enumerate the works that enforce sparse intermediate motif activations in an end-to-end neural architecture to make localized concepts or biological motifs interpretable. Exclude sparse communication graphs, modularity alone, post-hoc symbolic explanations, papers merely mentioning sparsity, proceedings and duplicate versions. Describe each work's interpretable intermediate representation.

input_cases.grading_notes: Category: enumeration; expected_unique_works: 4. Full list: (1) Faceted Execution of Policy-Agnostic Programs, DBLP_conf_plas_AustinYFS13.pdf — faceted semantics for Jeeves propagates multiple views of sensitive values and provides termination-insensitive noninterference; PDF p.1 and sections 2–3. (2) Precise, Dynamic Information Flow for Database-Backed Applications, DBLP_conf_pldi_YangHASFC16.pdf, identical alias DBLP_journals_corr_YangHASFC15.pdf — Jacqueline enforces policies across application and relational database operations; PDF p.1 and core-language/framework sections. (3) Liquid Information Flow Control, DBLP_journals_pacmpl_PolikarpovaSYIH20.pdf, identical alias DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16.pdf — liquid types statically check expressive policies and localize/synthesize repairs; PDF p.1 and sections 3.1–3.3. (4) PICACHV: Formally Verified Data Use Policy Enforcement for Secure Data Analytics, actually DBLP_conf_popl_YangYS12.pdf — relational-algebra query-plan monitor with Coq proofs and trusted-execution support; PDF pp.1–2 and framework sections. PICACHV must be included even though its authors and actual 2025 content differ from what the filename suggests. Do not invent a separate original Jeeves POPL paper from this misleading filename. Count the Jacqueline and Lifty aliases once; do not treat the older-looking Lifty filename as an independent 2016 work. MANTRA generates benchmark compliance checks, not a sensitive-data policy-enforcement language/runtime, and fairness concentration verification is not data confidentiality enforcement.
input_cases.question: Across ResearchPapers, enumerate every distinct standalone method paper that automatically enforces declarative confidentiality, information-flow, or data-use policies for sensitive application data. Include language semantics, database-aware enforcement, static type-driven repair, and relational-query runtime monitors, but exclude fairness-only analysis, generic compliance benchmark generation, standards, proceedings and duplicate versions. Identify papers from their contents, not their filenames, and explain where each policy is enforced.

The Counterfeit Conundrum: Can Code Language
Models Grasp the Nuances of Their Incorrect
Generations?
Alex Gu gua@mit.edu
MIT CSAIL
Wen-Ding Li⋆ wl678@cornell.edu
Cornell University
Naman Jain⋆ naman jain@berkeley.edu
University of California, Berkeley
Theo X. Olausson ⋆ theoxo@csail.mit.edu
MIT CSAIL

Cornell University
Koushik Sen ksen@berkeley.edu
University of California, Berkeley
Armando Solar-Lezama asolar@csail.mit.edu
MIT CSAIL
Abstract
While language models are increasingly more proficient at code generation, they still
frequently generate incorrect programs. Many of these programs are obviously wrong,
but others are more subtle and pass weaker correctness checks such as being able to
compile. In this work, we focus on these counterfeit samples: programs sampled from
a language model that 1) have a high enough log-probability to be generated at a
moderate temperature and 2) pass weak correctness checks. Overall, we discover that
most models have a very shallow understanding of counterfeits through three clear
failure modes. First, models mistakenly classify them as correct. Second, models are
worse at reasoning about the execution behaviour of counterfeits and often predict their
execution results as if they were correct. Third, when asking models to fix counterfeits,
the likelihood of a model successfully repairing a counterfeit is often even lower than
that of sampling a correct program from scratch. Counterfeits also have very unexpected
properties: first, counterfeit programs for problems that are easier for a model to solve
are not necessarily easier to detect and only slightly easier to execute and repair. Second,
counterfeits from a given model are just as confusing to the model itself as they are to
other models. Finally, both strong and weak models are able to generate counterfeit
samples that equally challenge all models. In light of our findings, we recommend that
care and caution be taken when relying on models to understand their own samples,
especially when no external feedback is incorporated.
⋆ Equal contribution, author order determined via random.shuffle

6 Related Work
Language models as judges and verifiers
LLMs are increasingly explored for their potential
in evaluation and verification tasks in various do-
mains. In open-ended question answering, Zheng
et al. (2023) demonstrate that models like GPT-
4 align with human preferences, indicating their
potential as tools for assessing LLM-generated re-
sponses.
In domains like mathematics and commonsense
reasoning, various forms of automated LLM feed-
back have led to improved reasoning abilities
(Cobbe et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2023; Weng et al.,
2022; Lightman et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023;
Wang et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2024). Additionally,
Studies like (Schneider et al., 2023; Matelsky et al.,
2023) investigate LLMs as auto-graders or judges
for educators. On the other hand, Valmeekam et al.
(2023); Tyen et al. (2023); Stechly et al. (2023);
Chen et al. (2024b) find that LLMs can struggle to
find when they are wrong and that critiquing plans
could harm performance.
Evaluation and verification for code synthesis
The challenge of LLMs producing incorrect code
in response to natural language prompts has led
to a significant focus on automated evaluation and
verification of generated code samples. Various
studies have demonstrated that postprocessing the
samples from LLMs can substantially enhance the
accuracy of the system (Chen et al., 2022; Ridnik
et al., 2024; Key et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023b;
Li et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2023a).
Also, Inala et al. (2022); Zhang et al. (2023d);
Ni et al. (2023) have employed a neural model to
verify code samples, with the aim of ranking more
accurate codes higher.
Code understanding in language models Many
benchmarks evaluate aspects of code understand-
ing and code intelligence such as code summariza-
tion (Iyer et al., 2016; Hasan et al., 2021), commit
message generation (Liu et al., 2020), code compre-
hension (Singhal et al., 2024), clone detection (Lu
et al., 2021), code question answering (Sahu et al.,
2022), and code explaining (Muennighoff et al.,
2023). Neural-based code execution has been stud-
ied in (Austin et al., 2021; Nye et al., 2021; Gu
et al., 2024; La Malfa et al., 2024), and code repair
has been studied in (Madaan et al., 2023; Chen
et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2023a; Olausson et al.,
2024), and Liu et al. (2024) examine a suite of code
reasoning benchmarks.
A few controlled studies highlight the extent to
which language models understand code. For ex-
ample, code generation abilities have been shown
to drop after syntactic changes like identifier swaps
(Miceli-Barone et al., 2023) and semantic changes
like 1-indexing (Wu et al., 2023). Dinh et al. (2024)
show that models fail at completing code with bugs.
Jin and Rinard (2023) provide evidence that LMs
can learn meaningful representations when trained
on programs, Zhang et al. (2023c) explore the be-
havior of transformers to simulate recursive func-
tions, and Min et al. (2023) discover that code lan-
guage models are inconsistent on various coding
tasks.
Models understanding their own generations
Some recent works investigate the extent to which
models understand their generations. Huang et al.
(2023b); Chen et al. (2024a); Tyen et al. (2023);
Olausson et al. (2024) find that LLMs struggle to
find their own reasoning errors, but are able to cor-
rect them with adequate external feedback. Singhal
et al. (2024) discover that models are better at fix-
ing buggy code than distinguishing between correct
and buggy code. Relevant to our work, West et al.
(2023) and Oh et al. (2024) argue that generative
capability may not be contingent on understanding
capability in textual domains.
7 Conclusion
In this work, we bring attention to the counterfeit
samples of a code language model: incorrect pro-
grams that a model thinks are correct and can pass
surface-level correctness checks. We observe that

example of each, deferring more to Appendix F. For conciseness and readability, some of the

The Counterfeit Conundrum: Can Code Language
Models Grasp the Nuances of Their Incorrect
Generations?
Alex Gu gua@mit.edu
MIT CSAIL
Wen-Ding Li⋆ wl678@cornell.edu
Cornell University
Naman Jain⋆ naman jain@berkeley.edu
University of California, Berkeley
Theo X. Olausson ⋆ theoxo@csail.mit.edu
MIT CSAIL
Celine Lee⋆ cl923@cornell.edu
Cornell University
Koushik Sen ksen@berkeley.edu
University of California, Berkeley
Armando Solar-Lezama asolar@csail.mit.edu
MIT CSAIL
Abstract
While language models are increasingly more proficient at code generation, they still
frequently generate incorrect programs. Many of these programs are obviously wrong,
but others are more subtle and pass weaker correctness checks such as being able to
compile. In this work, we focus on these counterfeit samples: programs sampled from
a language model that 1) have a high enough log-probability to be generated at a
moderate temperature and 2) pass weak correctness checks. Overall, we discover that
most models have a very shallow understanding of counterfeits through three clear
failure modes. First, models mistakenly classify them as correct. Second, models are
worse at reasoning about the execution behaviour of counterfeits and often predict their
execution results as if they were correct. Third, when asking models to fix counterfeits,
the likelihood of a model successfully repairing a counterfeit is often even lower than
that of sampling a correct program from scratch. Counterfeits also have very unexpected
properties: first, counterfeit programs for problems that are easier for a model to solve
are not necessarily easier to detect and only slightly easier to execute and repair. Second,
counterfeits from a given model are just as confusing to the model itself as they are to
other models. Finally, both strong and weak models are able to generate counterfeit
samples that equally challenge all models. In light of our findings, we recommend that
care and caution be taken when relying on models to understand their own samples,
especially when no external feedback is incorporated.

In §6, we explained how abstract rewriting is similar to narrowing, but different in an important
way. There is a long tradition in narrowing of proving lifting lemmas similar to our own; the first
comes from Hullot [1980].
In App. E, we discuss the use of several terms similar to “abstract matching” in the contexts of
abstract interpretation of logic programs, model-checking, and term-rewriting engines, as well as
several minor uses of syntactic abstraction.
Control-Flow Analysis. Many papers have been written on control-flow analysis [Jagannathan and
Weeks 1995; Jones 1981; Midtgaard 2012; Shivers 1991]. Older research tries to manually construct
a complicated analysis of programs with highly-dynamic control flow. Our work automatically
constructs CFG-generators from first principles. Our goal is not to analyze complex programs, but
to match the work of hand-written CFG-generators with minimal user input.
As such, we do not consider this work as part of the literature on control-flow analysis. Owing to
their different emphasis, these works uniformly have three limitations that make them unsuitable
for automatically deriving CFG-generators:
(1) While they explain how a human could define a new analysis for different languages, their
analyses are ultimately manually defined for each language. They further repeat this manual
construction for every abstraction used.
(2) They check that their result safely approximates executions, but pay no attention to the shape
of the graph.
(3) Most importantly, they manually partition program states into equivalence classes. That is, they
manually annotate the program with labels or program-points, using these as CFG nodes. This
is a hindrance to both automation and theory, as most type theories do not contain labels. A
major motivation of this work is to support our ongoing work on combining analyses with
different notions of program point (i.e.: partition program states differently), which makes not
hardcoding them especially important.
App. E gives a brief overview of control-flow analysis, and discusses two works that deserve special
mention, due to use of abstract machines and focus on generality.
9 CONCLUSION
This work presented both an algorithm for constructing CFGs from first principles and the world’s
first CFG-generator generator. Yet our work also furthers three larger goals.
First, we have provided an answer to “what is a control-flow graph?” beyond the vague “a CFG is
an abstraction of control-flow:” A CFG is a projection of the transition graph of abstracted abstract

Second, we have introduced abstract rewriting as a simple yet powerful technique for deriving

Third, we have used a language’s semantics to derive a tool entirely unlike a semantics. Though

Through further analysis, we find that counterfeit samples have other unexpected properties (Sec.
4). We find, for example, that counterfeit samples from problems that are easier for the model
to solve are not easier to assess and only slightly easier to execute and repair, highlighting an
inconsistency between generation and understanding capabilities. We also observe that models
don’t perceive their own counterfeit samples differently from other models’ counterfeits and that
models of all capability levels are able to generate equally difficult counterfeit samples.
Overall, we find that these counterfeit samples are, in a sense, adversarial to the model: models
often struggle to assess their correctness, reason about their execution as if they were correct
programs, and repair them at a low rate. Understanding counterfeit samples is a prerequisite to
many downstream applications in which models use their own feedback to improve themselves.
Therefore, in light of our findings, we recommend exercising caution in these schemes such
as self-repair and model-based reranking of outputs, especially when no external feedback is
incorporated.
2 Experimental Setup
2.1 Generating Counterfeit Examples
We use three datasets: HumanEval, LeetCode, and ODEX (Wang et al., 2022b). HumanEval
evaluates code generation of simple natural language descriptions, LeetCode is a harder dataset
of the same flavor using programming interview practice problems, and ODEX tests knowledge
of diverse Python libraries. To generate counterfeit examples, we first sample programs from
CodeLlama (CL), DeepSeek-Coder Instruct (DS-I), and StarCoder (SC) at temperature T = 0.6.
Of the incorrect programs, we design a dataset-specific filter to remove incorrect programs that
do not pass mild correctness criteria. For HumanEval, counterfeits are programs passing at least
10% of EvalPlus (Liu et al., 2023) tests. For LeetCode, counterfeits are programs that received a
“Wrong Answer” verdict, which filters out programs that crashed during runtime or took too long
to finish. For ODEX, counterfeits are programs that can be successfully parsed by ast.parse and
are under 500 characters. In Fig. 2, we show the number of counterfeits generated by different
models (left), benchmarks (middle), and problem difficulty levels (right), showing that counterfeits
are widespread and occur in each setting.
2.2 Code Understanding Tasks
We evaluate counterfeits on the following tasks:
Correctness Checking: The goal is to check whether a model-generated Python program (either correct
or counterfeit) correctly implements a natural language (NL) specification. These specifications
often include input-output examples. We use CoT with majority voting (Wei et al., 2022; Wang
et al., 2022a) and report accuracy.
Execution Prediction: The goal is to predict the execution output of a given model-generated Python
program on a specific input. We use an execution-based metric for correctness and report pass@1,
the fraction of samples that are correct.

We provide empirical evidence that code language models have a shallow understanding of these
counterfeit samples (Sec. 3) via three evaluations: correctness checking, execution prediction, and
program repair. For correctness checking, the model is asked to assess whether a short piece
of code correctly implements a natural language specification (sometimes with test cases). For
execution prediction, the model is given a program-input pair and asked to predict the output
of executing the program on the given input. For fairness, we ensure the programs are generally
short and that execution does not require complex calculations. For repair, the model is given the
counterfeit program alongside its original specification and is asked to correct it. First, we find
that models frequently misjudge counterfeit samples as correct. Second, models are much worse
at reasoning about the execution of counterfeits than their correct companions, often executing
counterfeits as if their semantics matched those of a correct program. Third, models falter at repair:
the likelihood of a model successfully repairing a counterfeit example is often even lower than that
of generating a correct program when sampling from scratch. As a caveat, this paper focuses on
open-source models, primarily CodeLlama 34B and DeepSeek Instruct 33B. We also present limited
results on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 which suggest that GPT-3.5 behaves similarly to the open-source

more generally in language models, which is con-
sistent with the findings from West et al. (2023).
Because models being able to understand their own
counterfeit samples is a prerequisite to strong self-
repair and self-verification schemes, we recom-
mend that others be critical and careful in light
of our findings.
8 Limitations
We identify a few limitations below:
Vague labels for HumanEval samples : We
find that HumanEval specifications can often be
vague with the inputs and outputs that are tested
on. Therefore, some programs can be argued to
be either correct or counterfeit. When manually
inspecting programs and their scores, we find that
base tests are too weak while EvalPlus tests are too
strong. Therefore, for correctness, we use the crite-
ria that the program must pass all base samples and
at least 95% of EvalPlus samples. However, this
only affects a small fraction of samples and we do
not believe changes any of our main claims (which
are also supported by LeetCode and ODEX).
Filter for counterfeit samples: In this work, we
use a relatively liberal filter for counterfeit samples
that consists of mostly basic syntax and/or correct-
ness checks. While we believe our results would
hold for slight alterations of our filter, we do not
assess this.
Nature of counterfeit samples: The scope of
this work is limited to counterfeit samples that are
generated by sampling from a natural language de-
scription. It is unclear how these samples differ
from human-written incorrect samples or samples
constructed in a different way, for example by syn-
thetically injecting bugs into correct samples as in
HumanEvalFix (Muennighoff et al., 2023).
Dataset and prompting variation: While we
make a best-effort attempt to use standardized
prompts that lead to the best performance, eval-
uation has been found to be quite sensitive to the
prompt and task format (Mizrahi et al., 2023). In
addition, there is variation across the datasets gen-
erated by various models. We try to mitigate this
by showcasing that our conclusions remain robust
across a variety of datasets and models.
Other perspectives on code understanding :
Although the three tasks we evaluate capture im-
portant aspects of code understanding, our claims
do not necessarily extrapolate to other aspects of
code understanding such as code summarization,
translation, or optimization. We believe that other
dimensions of code understanding are equally im-
portant and encourage future evaluation beyond the
tasks we present here.
Limited results for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4: All
our counterfeit samples are generated from CodeL-
lama, DeepSeekInstruct, and StarCoder, so it is un-
known whether the same insights apply to GPT-3.5
